title: Conveyor Jam
description: Clear and recover from a conveyor jam condition

n1.text: Both sensors are showing product present — that means something's stuck or backed up. Can you see where the jam is? Look at the transfer points and anywhere the belt changes direction.
n1.hint: Most jams happen at transfer points, diverters, or where product enters/exits the conveyor.

options.label: Yes, I can see the jam
options.transition: Good, you found it. Let's get it cleared safely.

options.label: No, nothing obvious
options.transition: OK, might be a sensor issue then. Let's check.

n2.text: Stop the conveyor before clearing the jam. Is the jam something you can clear by hand, or is product wedged in tight?
n2.hint: If product is wedged under a guard or between rollers, don't force it — you could damage the belt or the product.

options.label: It's wedged in tight
options.transition: Don't force it. Let's do this properly.

n3.text: Let's check if it's a sensor problem rather than an actual jam. Can you see the sensor indicators? Both sensors should have their LEDs on. Wave your hand in front of each one — do the LEDs respond?
n3.hint: Photoelectric sensors have an indicator LED that changes when the beam is blocked or reflected. Proximity sensors light up when metal is near.

options.label: Sensors respond normally
options.transition: Sensors are working. The jam might be downstream causing a backup.

options.label: One or both sensors seem stuck
options.transition: Sensor issue — that explains the false jam signal.

n4.text: Check downstream — is the next conveyor or machine station running? A backup from downstream will pile things up here.
n4.hint: If the downstream equipment is stopped or full, product has nowhere to go.

options.label: Downstream is stopped
options.transition: There's your root cause. This conveyor is fine — the problem is downstream.

options.label: Downstream is running
options.transition: Downstream is clear. Let's check product alignment.

n_clear.text: Clear the jam and you should be good to go.
steps: Stop the conveyor using the local stop button
Remove the jammed product by hand
Inspect the belt for any damage from the jam
Restart the conveyor and watch the first few products go through
If jams keep happening at the same spot, check the guide rail alignment

n_wedged.text: Product is wedged — don't muscle it out or you'll damage something. Let's do this right.
steps: Lock out and tag out the conveyor
Remove guards or covers to access the jam point
Carefully extract the jammed product (cut it out if needed)
Inspect the belt, rollers, and guides for damage
Check guide rail spacing — if product is catching, the rails may need adjustment
Replace guards and restart

n_sensor.text: Sensor is giving a false jam signal. This is a sensor alignment or wiring issue, not an actual jam.
steps: Clean the sensor lens — dust and debris cause false triggers on photoelectric sensors
Check sensor mounting — vibration can shift the alignment over time
Verify the sensor wiring connections are tight
Adjust the sensor sensitivity if it has a pot or teach button
If the sensor is damaged, replace it

n_downstream.text: The jam here is caused by a downstream backup. Fix the downstream issue and this conveyor will clear itself.
steps: Go check the downstream equipment — find out why it stopped
Clear any issues downstream first
Once downstream is running, product should flow through
If this happens frequently, consider adding accumulation logic to prevent backup jams

n_alignment.text: Product may be misaligned on the belt, causing it to catch on guides or at transfer points. This is usually a setup issue.
steps: Check product placement at the infeed — is it being placed straight on the belt?
Verify guide rail width and alignment along the full conveyor length
Look for any bent or damaged guide sections
If product shape has changed recently, the guides may need adjustment
